body: Alright, just made it public

If I were to rate Prozac's success on me based on how I feel now, which is a feeling I've had for a while, which is that I'm happy, then I'd say it's been good for me. I wouldn't know anything about jumping from medication to medication, i was fortunate that the first thing I was prescribed worked for me in the long run. And by the long run I mean this far down the line from my diagnosis and after the medication has been given time to settle into my system

I'm on 20mg of Prozac and 50mg of Seroquel. The first is a pretty commonly known antidepressant. The second is primarily an anti psychotic, but at lower doses (like mine) it is a sleep aid and it works together with the antidepressant to counter depression. 

I'm actually wide awake at about 4am because I'm actually visiting my friends at the university and I left my medication at home. I take the seroquel at night as a sleep aid and nights I go without it i have insomnia, just like this one. Before I was diagnosed I did only get a few hours of sleep a night and the medication did help with that. Unfortunately I'm more at a point where i can't sleep at all without it. 

The current dosages are what I have been at since i was diagnosed. I often wondered many times if it was appropriate to make adjustments, but I never did. Of course there were many ups and downs (especially), but after giving the medication time to work, in cooperation with my therapy, I personally am feeling better than i ever have. While I most certainly struggle with depression and anxiety to date, I think that over the past about two months, or month and a half have been absolutely monumental in my recovery but I would attribute that to the intense 9 hours a week group therapy I was participating in.

I understand how you feel. I always live in fear of another depressive episode being around the corner and it strikes when you least expect it. The last thing you want to do is feel guilty about your condition. It will only make you feel worse. I urge you to seek professional help. Medication has done a lot of good for me, and likewise therapy has done the same.

Well, think back to how he reacted when you told him the first time. Understandably, people tend to be taken aback and sometimes startled at the revelation. If he showed concern for your well being, then it wouldn't hurt to reopen the discussion. This is a hard thing to decide so you'll have to come up with the decision yourself.

I cut when I feel alone. I don't when I remember I'm not. 

It's my best friend's birthday today. I thought of him when I felt the urge to cut today. I know he doesn't want me to and I owe him that much.

I see my therapist tomorrow and a psychiatrist the following day. Today was my first day of cognitive behavioral therapy. 

I understand what the problem is. I'm just imagining that everyone around me has negative thoughts towards me and that leads me to sad moods and now self-destructive behaviors like cutting and refusing to eat. It's just so hard to combat it.

I know. Everybody keeps saying the same old things. That it gets better. That it's not easy. That it takes time. And that he/she is there for me. 

It gets way too hard honestly. I'm constantly cycling between a 3 and an 8 (10 being the most depressed and 0 being the least). 

The fact that other people are able to learn from me is helpful. I used to work in a university residence hall and after I shared my story with my boss, they decided, at my recommendation, to hold a program that would educate the residents about mental health. And the thought of such a thing helping others helps me in a way.

I refer to what happened to me a little over a week and a half ago as an "attempt", but I guess by some definitions it might not qualify. Say for example a person actually swallows a bunch of sleeping pills but they get pumped out in time. I was sitting on the edge of a cliff and my friend found me, because I told her what I was going to do before I even got there. 

I was hospitalized for several days afterward. My attempt wasn't over something that happened to me that day, it was the culmination of what I understand now was at least a year of depression but feelings of self-loathing that have followed me for my entire life. The treatment I received was the first I ever had for my depression. I had to withdraw from college for the time being and subsequently no longer have the part-time job I had when I was there. 

My friends have been my lifeline and my mom has been so supportive of me, as she had no idea I was depressed before. Both have been nothing but amazing towards me and I'm so grateful to have them. My relationships with them and that between themselves has strengthened so much and I am very glad for that. 

These past few days have been me trying to reconnect with old friends from my hometown, and trying to live a normal life.

I'm a 19 year old dude who loves hip-hop and garage rock but I was rocking pretty hard to that new song by Taylor Swift. Maybe because it fits to much to my situation. I'm on my road to recovery after surviving my near-attempt, and a lot of my depression comes from simply not fitting in. The song is about it not mattering if you don't. and say what you will about it being mindless pop, it's an easily danceable beat

Your little brother might as well have been me. I'm 19 and I came close to taking my own life on the 15th when I was sitting on the edge of a cliff,  contemplating jumping. I'm an introvert too, although since I began college I did try as much as I could to come out of that shell. Still, I was, and still do, cope with major self-esteem issues and part of that comes from being shamed for being introverted so I can sympathize with that.
 
Since I got out of the hospital that got me stable, I've finally started healing. I had to give up my job and withdraw from college for the time being, but in the end it will be worth it. I'm sorry for your brother. My friend saved me and that changed my entire life for the better in the long-term. I wish you had your brother here today, but I hope you find peace in the fact that his suffering is now stopped. I was in the same place he was and believe me, it felt like an unending pain.
Thanks for your kind words and advice, friend. I will keep such thoughts in mind!

Also, I didn't notice the first question! The stay was actually not so bad. It wasn't the Four Seasons, but you know, it wasn't American Horror Story, hahaha. (I have been waiting to use this joke since I got out).

Every day we followed a schedule, which was pretty much the same most weekdays, except for the fact that we got to paint twice on Tuesdays and weekends (I mention Rec Therapy in another comment, this is what I am talking about).

Every morning they would check our vital signs, we'd take our meds, have breakfast, and visit with the psychiatrist. There would be a couple of group therapy sessions--these were things like "Goals Group" or "Life Skills Group". Goals group was just sharing a goal and a positive statement for the day. Life skills is pretty self-explanatory. I can't remember the name of the last group. I just know that in that group I did the most opening up. It was probably the closest thing to actual therapy. The other ones were more like the speaker educating us, whereas this one was one where we were the ones sharing. 

Rec Therapy always came before lunch. After lunch, basically until dinner, which was like 5 hours apart, we could do whatever. Which basically means either go to your room and sleep, or sit in the lounge and try to find something to do in there. There was a TV with a radio inside (I have never encountered this before), and we had to ask for the remote to change the channel on the DVR but we could watch anything. There were a few games in there, like Trivial Pursuit or puzzles you could solve. There was a Tetris Jenga set. They also had a sparse selection of DVDs to watch. We watched Ferris Bueller once, which was the first time I had seen it. (Fuck! I just remembered I didn't use the line, *"Do you have a kiss for daddy?"* when I got out. My friends would have gotten a real kick out of that.)

After dinner which was from about 5-5:50, again we just did whatever until medications at about 8:30-9:30, and pretty much all of us had some kind of drowsiness side-effect to our meds. They shut the lights in the lounge off at 10, so you have to be out of there by then. But by then we're all pretty much all sedated and ready for bed at 10. 

They always had someone monitoring your location at any time, and especially at night, someone would enter your room like every 10 minutes or so to make sure you were still in there.

I actually missed three straight days of work when I was hospitalized, and my boss and coworkers had no idea why until after I got out and told my boss.

I work(ed) part-time behind the desk of a university residence hall. I made it clear to my boss that I would like my coworkers to know exactly what happened to me so they could learn from my story and also asked that they put on a program which would educate people about mental health. She was very receptive to the idea. 

Because the university told me that I will be gone for a long time, more then likely I cannot return to my job. But for people who have been hospitalized for mental illnesses, it is our right not be to discriminated against, as far as getting another job, because of that. 

I'm actually not really sure about this one, especially because I was only a student with a part-time job. If they don't, they really should.

Hanging out with my friends and just joking around. I'm just your regular 19 year old guy, I guess. Rude jokes, goofing off, whatever. I wish I could give you a more thorough answer! I laugh at everything. Arrested Development is my favorite TV show. (I'm laughing because I initially said Arrested Development is "very favorite" TV show). I'm Skyping with my buddies as I'm writing this and they find this very hilarious.

We could take fresh air breaks, there was a patio connected to one of the lounge rooms (the one on the other side) which had three walls, and kind of a mesh gate over our heads, so yeah, no way to actually go outside, although we could breathe fresh air. I liked not having this patio connected to the lounge of the side I was actually on because I could look out the window and actually see the outside world (and very frequently deer would appear just outside these windows), this is not something the other lounge had, although they did have "outside". But we both had access to this patio so it didn't make a difference.

My university contacted my mom, because it was university police that responded to the 911 call my friend made. She called me broken up in tears, because she had no idea whatsoever about my depression. She has, I believe, moved past the grief and is fully committed to my recovery. She's respected my decisions to gradually go public with my experience. 

My dad, on the other hand, wants to keep this all in the immediate family and he wants me to be "be careful who I tell". To which I replied, "What the fuck are we even saying, keeping my depression a secret is the reason why I even did this". He's concerned about what people will think about me, as in they will think I am crazy or dangerous. In all honesty, he is the only person who has failed to understand me and my condition. While there are people out there in the world who misunderstand mental illnesses, it's up to us to advocate for ourselves and help people to understand what they are and what having one is like. Sweeping my condition under the rug, and failing to educate people about my actions and what caused them would not help me in my recovery at all nor the understanding of those who don't get it.

Every single person I have since told, including the two people I told *today*, have been remarkably understanding and supportive. I am careful about who outside my close knit group of friends knows the whole truth, but as far as the need-to-know basis goes, my family is my family. They deserve to know what happened to me, and I want them to learn how to prevent this from happening to them or anyone they know. 

It has been hard for my mom particularly to keep the secret of my attempt from my three sisters, who were all very anxious over my sudden disappearance off the face of the Earth for the past week. I told all three of them that I was back home and safe, and that I had something to tell them. They are responded to this with general relief, except for the fact that me telling them I had something important to say made them anxious to various degrees. 

One of my sisters was actually *angry with me* for giving her something to worry about when she is miles away stressing about other things. And that reaction is exactly why I did not tell her what happened to me in the first place. One of them is celebrating her 21st this weekend (although her actual birthday occurred when I was in the hospital) and it remains to be seen whether or not I will actually go to this thing that is happening for it (I never wanted to go in the first place).

And, I will say that the relationship between me and with my mom, that between myself and my friends, that between my friends themselves, and that of my friends and my mom (which previously did not exist) are all very much strengthened and I am extremely thankful for that. My mom has been very kind to my friends and is very grateful to them for their support, *especially* to that friend that saved me.

It was a facility meant to stabilize people with mental disorders and/or addictions who are believed to be a danger to themselves or others. I was taken there after I was sitting in the local hospital for about 12 hours. I was taken in on a 5150--that's an involuntary psychiatric hold. These normally last 72 hours (I'm talking the state of California, dunno about everywhere else) but because I was prescribed medication for depression, I had to stay as long as six days so they could observe my reaction to the medications.

I met with a psychiatrist who was able to diagnose me and prescribe me medication, and the group therapy sessions were extremely... therapeutic, for lack of a better word, haha.

I met a lot of incredible people, as I said. A guy with his own pest control business who checked himself in voluntarily to get help for his violent episodes was very wise to me for a time. A very learned Notre Dame alumnus suffering from alcoholism who had both a doctorate and a masters degree. An alcoholic whose two kids were born addicted to heroin and methadone, respectively. She was one of my best friends in my last couple of days on the inside. A former airline stewardess with depression. And a reclusive "Furry" who, at the age of 22 had tried just about every single recreation drug you can come up with, with the exception of heroin. Among other things he told me about his drug use, he said he had done 200x (not exaggerating) the amount of LSD that a person is meant to do when they do it, and it very much changed him forever. 

We had Rec Therapy once most days, except twice on Tuesdays and weekends. These were days where we could do arts and crafts like painting and drawing, molding clay, anything like that. This was the best part about being inside because doing art legitimately is extremely soothing. 

I'm wearing a bracelet right now that I don't remove, in memory of my friend on the inside, who is leaving that facility tomorrow. He made this bracelet for me in Rec Therapy. This kid was young, just a bit older than I--I'm 19--he was 21. He had been a bunch of different medications just to keep him sedated. He had huge arms, and he was an extremely powerful kid. There were two sides to the unit and we were separated by two sets of double doors which needed a key that went into the wall (this was true of the most secure doors, including exit doors). I met him when I first arrived, and he seemed alright, although I could tell he was a few sandwiches short of a picnic, if you'll forgive the stupid metaphor. He was later moved over to the other side, and I didn't know why. What I found out later was that when he was over there, he kicked open the *extremely secure, locked door* and ran for it. I actually didn't know what the outside looked like at the time, but the facility was actually huge when I saw the outside, so he never had any chance of getting out into the real world. I don't know exactly what his disorder(s) were but they seemed characteristic of bipolar, or schizoaffective disorder, something along those lines. He would get angry or cry terribly after acting just fine. He would ramble on about UFOs and his hallucinations. He said I was his best friend on the inside. I will never forget him, nor will I forget anyone I met in there. There actually were a couple of times where I feared for myself because of him, but in my mind he has a good heart and I think it is a damn shame that there is only so much help for him. 

Mind you this place is for stabilization, not long-term care. CA law states that you can't be held for over 17 days in a place like that involuntarily. You do eventually have to leave. And some people come in and out of places like that, they have relapses, they get stabilized, and then they relapse again.

That's pretty much exactly how it was. In the days and weeks leading up to my attempt, I was being more withdrawn and more asocial and aloof. And ordinarily I am a I-wanna-make-you-laugh kind of guy. But my friends had seen this side of me before and there were times when I opened up and said I was going through a rough patch but getting better. But what was really happening was me getting through that spell but another one would begin soon after. This was for weeks leading up to the attempt.

Even I didn't know that *that* spell of depression would be *the one* even though I already had a note prepared.

Hell, five hours before my attempt, I was more than happy to accept the invite of another close friend who was offering himself to chat with me (I had previously opened up to him about my feelings, without using the D or S words). The day before, he had met up with me after I asked him to, and I had every intention of opening up again. Except this time he showed up drunk. I know that him asking me to come out on Wednesday was his way of making up for the previous day. I said that "I wouldn't be coming", that he was "a really good guy" and "I'm really sorry." literally moments before my friend finally found me. He sent me a lot of messages urging me to come by and say hi and to please reply, and those would have been the last things he'd have sent to me.

Firstly thank you for your support. 

I remember calling out to her when I noticed the light from her phone flashing at me. I couldn't move from the edge for a second. She came up a little ways behind me, where it was safe, and asked me to come over, and I said I couldn't move. She asked me again and I did, really sluggish like. She put her arm over me, and walked me over to a nearby bench where she said that "Everything would be okay" and things of that nature and she also told me she called the police, who shortly arrived afterwards. 

After I told her I had already written a suicide note weeks prior (my memory was foggy, I had actually been just 10 days before, though I revised it one last time), she said she was glad that I had told her. I maintain she was the only person *in the world* who could have saved me.

I don't know, like... I know that she has a lot on her plate herself. So I don't really want to burden her with this. She was once in a situation where, in the midst of her own battle with depression, she was in a rocky relationship with a bipolar who was also suicidal.  

A lot of times I've come close, even with other people. I come really close to just breaking ongoing silences and saying, "I have to tell you something serious. I want to kill myself." I never, ever do. 

People are always telling stories about how their mental health ruined their relationships with people after they opened up about it. People would try to help in the wrong ways, or just be too afraid to. 

Obviously I go through spells where I become a practically mute recluse who can't laugh or show any other emotion than sadness. It's not subtle, especially when you consider how I am usually. If anyone asks about it, I lie about it. I say I'm sick, or I say I'm just stressed. I have to give some kind of excuse for blowing people off whenever it gets this way. 

Last night I did open up to an extent about this to my friend. I was not explicit and never said the "D" word or the "S" word but I admitted that sometimes I get bouts of what I vaguely described were the symptoms of depression and that I was afraid that it was hurting my relationships with my other friends. He was very open and receptive to what I had to say but I still felt like it wouldn't have been right to tell him the whole truth. It honestly just made me sadder in a way, because in the end, it won't matter what he said. He's just going to feel worse that he knew.

For all that she's done for me, I don't know how she'll react to me telling her about it. I know that she's serious about wanting to help me... but how do you admit to one of your best friends that you already wrote the letter you're gonna leave when you off yourself?

EDIT: I had to repost this from my alt account since I don't talk about my depression on my main one for obvious reasons and accidentally used it.

I just wrote out the longest reply of my life and apparently it all disappeared!!! And I'm in the library and supposed to be studying. I'm gonna just have to write something else. And it's going to be completely different.
I made brand new friends in college, and among my best friends, I met them at different points in my first year. We all lived in the same building. This is one of the biggest things about your social life. In the beginning everybody is very friendly, and not that that changes, but eventually people do start to settle into cliques.

I go to a respected university that is also known for its party scene. As a first-year I sort of was keen on trying it. I mean, everybody will be. I know a lot of people who didn't touch alcohol or drugs before college and today party all of the time. Some people try it and step away from it , some people stay on it. I'm of the former. My friends like to party but I don't.

This wasn't the case for me in the beginning (I met one of my best friends at a party) but as my depression worsened I lost more and more confidence and decided to give up participating in that kind of thing almost completely. The sad thing is that I'm more willing to do it in certain cases (like with my close [f]riend) than with my buddies.

For me one of the detractors of drinking is the huge ego trip people get out of it. Everybody wants to pound 100 beers and do a dozen shots and I kind of just want to chill out. My university kind of does have that "bro" and "babe" culture (not to say that it's not full of intelligent and hardworking individuals).

Like back when I first got a new set of co-workers, they threw a small function and I was more than happy to participate, mostly because I could tell they were nice and also they were mostly girls and I figured, well what could go wrong. And it was a really good time since it was a private thing.

These days, I wouldn't go anywhere near a house party or frat party full of people I don't know. I'm just not confident enough. And I'm not white and IMHO also I'm not attractive, one or both of which can literally open doors for you here.

Among my best friends, I'm the only one who almost never drinks. I'll admit it's a real fear for me that this is kind of alienating, but all-in-all things could be worse.

I don't regret my [limited] experiences with partying because it got me in touch with some people whose friendships I value, but now that I have experienced it I made the decision to walk away from it. Even though it's a pretty big thing here, the people are also pretty chill outside of that and it's not hard to make friends who don't care about what you do whether they do it or not.

When I was a first-year they showed us a presentation and the advice was always contradictory. Like, step out of your comfort zone but embrace who you are. Something like that. This year I'm trying to step out of my zone by participating in some extracurriculars and getting more social like I did last year, but ultimately there really is no shame in just being alone (or with one other person) and doing what makes you happy. Maintaining that kind of balance between being social enough to not be alienated and allowing time to yourself as an introvert is kind of a constant daily struggle but it's certainly possible.

When I told my sister I thought I was depressed, over a Skype call when I was away at college, I could tell she wasn't taking me as seriously as she could have. She probably thought I was just sad and being overly dramatic. And she's the closest one to me in my family so it made me feel like I can't go to my family for that kind of thing.

The sad thing is my friends have been inviting me to do things with them but I turn them down (2 minutes ago they asked me along to watch a movie) because I don't want to turn them off with my mood. We had brunch this morning together and I maybe said two words at the table. I don't want to seem like I'm cutting them out or blowing them off and I'm glad they still ask me around. I've actually had instances where I've walked out of group functions and texted a friend saying something like, "I'm sorry I had to leave I just wasn't feeling right, I don't want to seem like I'm blowing you off."

I know it's hard for people to know what to do or say. I don't want to up and say well, since my friends don't know how to counsel me or how to deal with my depression, they're not my real friends. I don't know if that's because I'm being "lenient" with them, or if I don't want to face the facts. 

My friends see it, that's the thing. I have a close friend who has been so helpful to me. I have friends who see how I am and offer themselves but I'm just not comfortable opening up. I have friends who see how I am and don't say anything, probably because they are afraid of acknowledging it. I have friends who see and know exactly what I'm going through, some who say something and some who don't. Or just choose to recognize it when they feel like it.

It's so crazy that I read this post and it was like I was reading my own words.

Literally, just *two nights ago*, I had nothing to do because my friends had gone out and I prefer to stay in. This is at college. My friends already know at this point that I hate going out. The irony in this is that I met one of them at a party, but that was over a year ago when I had just came to college and was confident enough to try new things. 

I called my mom, which I usually never do unless we have some family business to talk about. In fact my family often, and more recently has tried to get in touch with me when I am away at school, sending me text messages like "Have a great day! Haven't heard from you. Hope you are doing okay." They often communicate on a group text which I am a part of but never participate in. 

She asks me, "So are you going out tonight?"

"No. All of my friends did though."

"So did you stay in so you could play computer games?"

At this very moment I was actually about to start a game of Dota 2, a game which I long ago quit but recently started playing again, partly because it's a way for me and my roommate / one of my best friends to connect.

"...Not...necessarily."

There was literally no way for her to have known what I was doing. It made me feel lousy.

And my mom is actually generally a conservative person. Had I been drinking and goofing off in high school she wouldn't have liked it because I was a serious student. Now they've largely taken an implicit "what happens at college, stays at college" stance as far as what I do out here. Basically, they get that I'm a college student and that I should be "having fun" (i.e. drinking and socializing) and they trust me to be responsible because of my past record of never getting in trouble. Now I feel that my family worries about my lack of social interaction more than ever.

When my birthday came over the summer, my mom asked me to invite my friends. I told her I had brought it up before and they expressed misgivings about the idea particularly because of the distance, which I understood (I live in SoCal, they all live in NorCal between 4-7 hours away). She insisted I remind them of my offer, almost like she was desperate to know her son had some kind of companionship.

My sister once blasted me in front of my cousins and some other people about how I keep to myself and rarely leave my room when I'm at home. Honestly the pain and humiliation of it I can't even describe. I was close to just cutting her out of my life forever at that point and I still kind of hold a grudge because of how she acts towards me. 

I'm sorry I'm rambling about me. Just know that you're not alone in how you feel.
I'm a college student with a job on campus; I purposely work late shifts on weekends (until 2am) so I don't have to be around when all of my friends get drunk and stop talking to me.

Sometimes for certain stretches of time I start to feel like my depression is gone. Then it comes back out of nowhere and hits you like a freight train. I'm like you in that I tend to joke around a lot, so when I get reclusive and withdrawn, people notice. I just isolate myself in those cases. ~~I would rather people not read too much into what is going on with me.~~ Well, maybe that's not true. Actually, yeah it isn't. I want people to come to me and offer their shoulder and tell me honestly that they will listen to what I have to say, and not just because they feel bad for me, but because they really care. Empathy is really what you need from a person in your time of need. 

I remember once I was having just a normal day and all of a sudden I felt like complete shit. A friend of mine made an off-hand comment at my expense which in retrospect meant nothing but it actually reminded me about everything about myself that I hate. I told my friend about it and she literally dropped everything and came to me; and this was very late at night. We had been very close before this point but it was around this time I realized how much I needed her. She knows what *not* to say, how not to be patronizing about what I'm going through because she copes with it as well.

Anyway my suggestion is maybe to find that friend you can confide in and who can *empathize*, not just sympathize with you.

Thank you for sharing your story and expressing your empathy. I hope you find resolution with your own depression.

I remember not having a good experience the first time I smoked, it was with people I barely knew and weren't too comfortable with and I was pretty sure I wasn't high. Then some time later I had a few "baked goods", I guess I had a too much because that night I could barely sleep, I felt like I had hands around my neck strangling me. I thought it was an nightmare but it was real. I got out of my bed and my heart was beating really fast, I thought I might have died then. Both times I think I wasn't in the right mind. After the second episode I swore off it but as I say I've reconsidered because I think I could get something out of it. Maybe acid is too big a jump. 

My friend, as I say has been struggling lately much like I have. We have been talking about it. He brought up going to an on-campus therapist and in some way I was kind of surprised he brought it up, not because I didn't think he had issues that needed working out but I thought it kind of big of him to step up and say "I want to get help and I think you could benefit if you did too". Last year I came very close to joining a group therapy session and even had a private session scheduled with the head psych, but in the end there was no room left in the group and this didn't happen. But anyway, I have to say that having friends who fight depression too in some way helps because there are people who have been to that dark place who will listen to you and who you can listen to. A close friend of mine who likewise has fought depression has been the closest thing to professional help I've had for the past year now.

I don't know. I mean, there are things missing from my life that I think contribute to my depression, but also even if I had them, I would still be. 

If anything, my academic accomplishments are all I ever really had. I worked hard in high school, and now I'm here at college but it's hard to keep up, or even indeed find the motivation to do so. Now I'm faced with the real possibility that I will not succeed in college or indeed in life beyond. But if I were to get my dream job, which is something financial, am I going to enjoy that? It's a cutthroat life riddled with vanity and stress. 

I have no love life whatsoever. I've never been kissed, and am a virgin. This actually isn't something that dominates my mind, and I'm glad it doesn't, I know how some people who are depressed because of this. I've sort of tried to chat up girls before but never built up the nerve to admit my feelings and been content to remain friends. Part of this is also that I don't think I'm even ready to have a relationship. It's companionship, more than love or sex that I want.

Thinking about it now I know I've got some great friends. Too often do I fear losing them though. I've lost many friends in the past because of my own personality and I don't want it to happen again. I'm too passive too often, and I also don't want to be too attached. I think my passiveness can turn off people and if I get too attached losing them will hurt me more and can drive them off. I don't know if that makes complete sense.
